title: Van guard: How Europe can kick its global diesel dependence – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: ECFR argues the EU should scrap an extra million old diesel vans in five years via a EUR 5,000 tax credit toward EU-made electric vans, costing about EUR 1bn per year, to cut diesel and crude import dependence while boosting European battery and auto demand.

insights.claim: More than 90% of EU diesel comes from EU refineries but nearly all the crude is imported, and EU diesel consumption is no lower than in 2007.
insights.speaker: Noah Gordon, Alex Turnbull
insights.so_what: Structural import exposure keeps European diesel prices tied to geopolitics.

insights.claim: Europe's 31 million vans make up about 10% of the vehicle fleet but burn 16% of its diesel, and the average van is almost 13 years old.
insights.speaker: Noah Gordon, Alex Turnbull
insights.so_what: Vans are a concentrated target for diesel demand reduction.

insights.claim: The Trump administration pressured Europeans to release diesel stocks or risk losing US diesel and lifted some sanctions on Russian diesel, while Spain and Germany cut diesel taxes amid the 2026 energy crisis.
insights.speaker: Noah Gordon, Alex Turnbull
insights.so_what: Diesel supply is now a geopolitical lever and a fiscal drain.
insights.locator: geopolitical cost of this diesel dependence

insights.claim: Europeans have spent an additional EUR 203m per day on diesel since the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.
insights.speaker: Noah Gordon, Alex Turnbull
insights.so_what: Quantifies the energy-shock cost that dwarfs the proposed programme.

insights.claim: Electric vans were 13% of new van sales in 2026 versus 6% in 2024, and a Volvo executive told the FT 'this is the end of diesel' for new sales in Europe.
insights.speaker: Noah Gordon, Alex Turnbull
insights.so_what: Supports the electrification trajectory for commercial vehicles.
insights.quote: this is the end of diesel

insights.claim: Proposed EU policy would cut new-van tailpipe CO2 by 90% by 2035 versus 2021 and the Clean Corporate Vehicles Regulation would mandate zero-emission shares in large corporate fleets by 2030, covering the roughly 90% of vans that are corporate.
insights.speaker: Noah Gordon, Alex Turnbull
insights.so_what: Regulatory pull for EV van demand and batteries.
insights.locator: EU policy is pushing that share higher

insights.claim: The authors propose a tax credit, for example EUR 5,000, for scrapping Euro 5 or older vans toward a new EU-made or partner-country electric van, costing about EUR 1bn per year over five years for a million vans.
insights.speaker: Noah Gordon, Alex Turnbull
insights.so_what: Potential demand catalyst for European EV van makers and battery supply chain.

insights.claim: A van scrappage scheme would give demand certainty to European batteries and could spur investment in weak links such as lithium iron phosphate cathode chemicals and processed graphite for anodes.
insights.speaker: Noah Gordon, Alex Turnbull
insights.so_what: Watch European cathode and anode materials as beneficiaries.
insights.locator: A van scrappage programme could provide demand certainty

insights.claim: Italy's roughly EUR 600m scrappage-linked EV bonus in 2025 was nearly fully subscribed within 24 hours, showing pent-up demand.
insights.speaker: Noah Gordon, Alex Turnbull

insights.claim: Scrappage schemes pull purchases forward, can subsidise the wealthy and have high cost per tonne of CO2, but the EU has accepted that climate policy need not pick only the cheapest technologies such as Chinese EVs.
insights.speaker: Noah Gordon, Alex Turnbull
insights.so_what: Industrial-policy motives, not cost efficiency, drive EU support.
